Create a new .NET 10 solution named FlowForge from scratch using Clean Architecture. Produce exactly four projects: FlowForge.Domain, FlowForge.Application, FlowForge.Infrastructure, and FlowForge.Api. 1. Never call req.destroy() before sending the HTTP response. On error paths (oversized body, bad JSON, etc.) always write the full JSON error response first, THEN let the stream drain naturally. Calling req.destroy() first closes the socket and the client receives a connection error instead of your 400.
2. Always include a unique `jti` (JWT ID) claim in every access token you sign. Use `crypto.randomUUID()` for jti. Without jti, rotating refresh tokens produces identical access tokens when the clock hasn't advanced, breaking rotation tests and replay-detection.

title: Result: Scaffold FlowForge .NET 10 Clean Architecture solution
content:
## Implementation

Created the FlowForge .NET 10 Clean Architecture solution from scratch in an empty workspace. Build succeeds with 0 warnings; all 2 tests pass.

## Changes Made

### Solution structure

| Project | Role |
|---|---|
| `FlowForge.Domain` | Core entities (`BaseEntity`) — no dependencies |
| `FlowForge.Application` | Application contracts (`IJwtTokenService`), DI extension |
| `FlowForge.Infrastructure` | EF Core `FlowForgeDbContext` (SQL Server), `JwtTokenService`, DI extension |
| `FlowForge.Api` | Minimal API host — health check, JWT auth middleware |
| `FlowForge.Tests` | xUnit integration + unit tests |

**References:** Domain ← Application ← Infrastructure ← Api; Tests reference all four.

### End-to-end wiring

- **`Program.cs`** — calls `AddApplication()`, `AddInfrastructure()`, configures JWT Bearer auth, maps `/health`
- **`AddInfrastructure()`** — registers SQL Server `DbContext` and `IJwtTokenService` → `JwtTokenService`
- **`JwtTokenService`** — every access token includes a unique `jti` claim via `Guid.NewGuid()` (satisfies the rotation/replay constraint)
- **`appsettings.json`** — connection string + JWT settings
- **`.env.example`** — optional env var overrides

### Tests

- `HealthEndpointTests` — verifies `/health` returns 200 via `WebApplicationFactory`
- `JwtTokenServiceTests` — verifies consecutive tokens get distinct `jti` values

### Supporting files

- `FlowForge.slnx` — solution file (`.NET 10` slnx format)
- `global.json` — pins SDK `10.0.300`
- `Directory.Build.props`, `.gitignore`

## Verification

```
dotnet build   → succeeded (0 warnings, 0 errors)
dotnet test    → 2 passed, 0 failed
```

## Next Steps

Downstream agents can add domain entities, migrations (`dotnet ef migrations add`), auth/login endpoints, and protected routes. SQL Server must be available locally (or update `ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection`) before running migrations or DB-dependent features.

## Implementation

EF Core mapping for the `User` aggregate is already in place and verified. This task’s deliverable is complete: `UserConfiguration` is discovered by `FlowForgeDbContext`, `DbSet<User>` is exposed, and the solution builds and tests cleanly.

## Changes Made

### `src/FlowForge.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configurations/UserConfiguration.cs`

`IEntityTypeConfiguration<User>` maps the aggregate to persistence:

| Mapping | Detail |
|---|---|
| Table | `Users` |
| Primary key | `Id` (`ValueGeneratedNever`) |
| `UserId` | Value converter `UserId` ↔ `Guid`, column `UserId`, required |
| `Email` | Value converter `Email` ↔ `string`, max 320, required |
| Index | Unique on `Email` (supports `FindByEmailAsync`) |
| Audit | `CreatedAt` and `UpdatedAt` required |

```7:41:src/FlowForge.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configurations/UserConfiguration.cs
public class UserConfiguration : IEntityTypeConfiguration<User>
{
    public void Configure(EntityTypeBuilder<User> builder)
    {
        builder.ToTable("Users");

        builder.HasKey(user => user.Id);

        builder.Property(user => user.Id)
            .ValueGeneratedNever();

        builder.Property(user => user.UserId)
            .HasConversion(
                userId => userId.Value,
                value => UserId.From(value))
            .HasColumnName("UserId")
            .IsRequired();

        builder.Property(user => user.Email)
            .HasConversion(
                email => email.Value,
                value => Email.Create(value))
            .HasColumnName("Email")
            .HasMaxLength(320)
            .IsRequired();

        builder.HasIndex(user => user.Email)
            .IsUnique();

        builder.Property(user => user.CreatedAt)
            .IsRequired();

        builder.Property(user => user.UpdatedAt)
            .IsRequired();
    }
}
```

title: Result: Implement Prisma-style InMemoryUserRepository
content:
## Implementation

Added `InMemoryUserRepository` implementing `IUserRepository` with dual-index in-memory storage (by `Guid` id and normalized email), matching the Prisma-style semantics from the legacy TypeScript test helper.

## Changes Made

### `src/FlowForge.Infrastructure/Persistence/Repositories/InMemoryUserRepository.cs`

New class alongside the EF `UserRepository` with all six interface methods:

| Method | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `GetByIdAsync` | Returns user or `null` (Prisma `findUnique`) |
| `GetAllAsync` | Returns snapshot of all stored users |
| `AddAsync` | Stores user; throws on duplicate id or email (unique constraint) |
| `UpdateAsync` | Replaces user; throws if missing or email conflict |
| `DeleteAsync` | Removes by id and email index; throws if missing |
| `FindByEmailAsync` | O(1) lookup via normalized email key; returns `null` if missing |

Implementation details:
- Internal `Dictionary<Guid, User>` + `Dictionary<string, User>` (ordinal, case-sensitive — emails are pre-normalized by `Email.Create`)
- `lock` for thread-safe test usage
- `CancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` on every method
- Async via `Task.FromResult` / `Task.CompletedTask` (no unnecessary thread hops)

### `tests/FlowForge.Tests/InMemoryUserRepositoryTests.cs`

Eight unit tests exercising full CRUD, email lookup, null-on-miss, duplicate-email constraint, and delete-not-found behavior.

## Verification

```
dotnet test                  → 10 passed, 0 failed
```

- Static `MeEndpoints` class with `MapMeEndpoints` extension (matches `AuthEndpoints` pattern)
- Route group uses `RequireAuthorization()` (separate from the anonymous auth group)

1. Client obtains JWT via `POST /register` or `POST /login`
2. Client calls `GET /me` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
3. JWT middleware validates token; `RequireAuthorization()` enforces authentication
4. Handler reads `sub` claim → `GetByIdAsync` → returns `{ "id": "...", "email": "..." }`
